description: 4 bear-steps or 12 chick-steps? Learn why we use centimetres, metres, kilograms and litres, read a ruler from zero, and see a small apple beat a big balloon.

youtube.title: Measure It! Length, Weight and Capacity for Kids | cm, kg, L | Grade 2 Math | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
Bear says the rug is 4 bear-steps. Chick says 12 chick-steps. Who is right? Both! That's why we use units everyone shares.
Measure with a ruler that starts at zero (and fix Robo's mistake), compare a big balloon and a small apple on a balance, and pour water to find out that a short, wide bowl holds more than a tall glass.
Try at home: measure a table with hand-spans, then with a ruler.

do.text: Measure It!
I measured the rug with my steps. Watch!
4 bear-steps!
I measured it too!
12 chick-steps!
4 or 12? You can't both be right... can you?
Maybe you both are. But why are the numbers different?
Look at their steps. A bear-step is big.
A chick-step is small. So Chick needs more steps.
Bigger steps, fewer steps. Smaller steps, more steps.
bear-steps
So they're both right in their own steps.
But that's confusing.
Exactly. If we all use the same size,
we all get the same answer!
Let's try the same little block for everyone.
10 blocks. Bear gets 10, Chick gets 10. Everyone agrees!
Grown-ups use the same units all over the world.
units
Like centimetres and metres?
Yes! Let's meet them.
Here is a ruler. Each number is one centimetre.
centimetre
Hold up a fingertip. It's about 1 centimetre wide!
The tall marks have numbers.
The spaces between are centimetres.
Let me measure this crayon.
It ends at 6. So it's 6 centimetres!
Wait. Where does the crayon start?
Um... at the 1?
Count the spaces, not the marks. From 1 to 6 is 5 spaces.
6 take away 1 is 5. It's 5 centimetres!
Put your finger on zero,
then count the jumps. That's the trick.
Let's slide it to start at zero.
It ends at 5. 5 centimetres! You were right.
When I say where does the ruler start, you say zero!
Where does the ruler start?
At zero! Great.
100 centimetres make 1 metre.
metre
Stretch your arms out wide. That's about 1 metre!
A door is about 2 metres tall.
Guess first, then measure. Here's a pencil.
Guess how long it is in centimetres.
It starts at zero and ends at 15. 15 centimetres!
Now a book. Guess first!
25 centimetres!
How much longer is the book? 25 take away 15.
10 centimetres longer.
And the rug? Let's use metre sticks.
One metre, two metres. The rug is 2 metres long!
2 m
A bear-step is about 50 centimetres.
4 of them make 2 metres.
Fun fact: you are a tiny bit taller in the morning!
Your back squashes a little during the day,
about 1 centimetre.
Now, how heavy is something? We use a balance.
weight
The heavier side goes down. The lighter side goes up.
I brought a big balloon!
And here's a small apple.
Hold out your hands like a balance.
Apple in one, balloon in the other.
Which side will go down?
The big balloon, or the small apple?
The apple goes down! The small apple is heavier.
But why? The balloon is so much bigger.
A balloon is mostly air inside thin rubber.
My balloon is so light, it almost floats away!
An apple is packed full inside.
Bigger is not always heavier!
We measure weight in kilograms.
kilogram
Fun fact: a 1 litre bottle of water weighs about 1 kilogram.
And tiny things use grams. A paper clip is about 1 gram.
My turn! I'm a heavy lifter.
Bear is much heavier than Chick. Kilograms tell us how much.
How much a container holds is called capacity.
capacity
We measure it in litres. This jug holds 1 litre.
litre
Here's a tall, thin glass full of water.
And a short, wide bowl full of water.
Which one holds more? Tall, or wide?
To be fair, we pour each one into the same jug.
Let's test! Pour the tall glass into the jug.
Only up to here. Let's mark the line.
Empty the jug. Now pour the wide bowl.
Wow! Much higher! The short, wide bowl holds more.
But why? The glass was taller.
The bowl is much wider, so there's more space inside.
Tall is not always more!
Fun fact: a teaspoon holds about 5 millilitres. A tiny unit!
March with me! Measure Mixer chant!
Ruler for long, scale for heavy,
jug for how much, measure-it ready!
Centimetres, metres, kilograms, litres!
Same for you and same for me,
that's how measuring should be!
Ruler for long, scale for heavy,
jug for how much, measure-it ready!
Challenge! Pick the tool and the unit.
We have a ruler, a scale, a jug and a metre stick.
How long is a crayon?
A ruler, in centimetres!
How heavy is a pumpkin?
A scale, in kilograms! A pumpkin is heavy.
How much milk is in a big bottle?
A jug, in litres!
Long things get a ruler.
Heavy things get a scale. Easy so far.
How far is it across the playground?
A metre stick or measuring tape, in metres!
How heavy is a feather?
A scale, in grams. Tiny!
Five for five. You picked every tool right.
In some countries,
people also use inches and feet. Same idea!
Quiz time! Which tool measures how heavy something is?
A scale or a balance!
A crayon goes from 0 to 8 on a ruler. How long is it?
8 centimetres!
Why do we use centimetres instead of bear-steps?
Steps are different sizes.
Centimetres are the same for everyone.
Does a bigger thing always weigh more?
No! The big balloon was lighter than the small apple.
Bear, Chick, how long is the rug?
2 metres!
Friends again. And everyone measured the same.
Measure something at home with a ruler. Bye!
